newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-IF KEEGAN FAILED, WHAT A GLORIOUS FAILURE.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-IF KEEGAN FAILED, WHAT A GLORIOUS FAILURE.

text.p: Kevin Keegan may have failed in his bid to win the English premier league title -- but if it was a failure, it was a glorious failure.

From his tiny stark office at Newcastle United's training ground near Durham, Keegan plotted a soccer revolution that transformed Newcastle from an ailing, decaying relic of a bygone era of glory, into the most exciting, attacking team in England.
He may have failed to win the title but he won over a million fans with the way his side played and helped Newcastle United win back its pride.
Keegan is an inspirational man who shrewdly used the tens of millions made available to him by Sir John Hall to build a team that last season came within a whisker of their first title since 1927.

But clearly the pressure of the job has taken its toll -- in much the same way as it did for Kenny Dalglish, who as a player filled Keegan's number 7 shirt when he replaced him at Liverpool. Dalglish quit midway through the 1990-91 season saying he needed a complete break from soccer. Keegan said much the same on Wednesaday.

The pressure began to tell in the run-in to last season's title when Keegan's nerve and that of his team cracked. Twelve points ahead of the field this time last year, Newcastle stumbled through the second half of the season to finish four points behind Manchester United, who went on to complete the domestic league and cup double.
Keegan had won the title before -- three times with Liverpool as a player in the 1970s -- and he finished his Liverpool career at the peak after they won the European Cup for the first time in 1977.

He joined Hamburg that year and became known to the German fans as Mighty Mouse. It was an apt nickname for a man who rose from humble surroundings in the Yorkshire village he once described as "a slum" to become a soccer millionaire honoured by the Queen.

He also transformed himself through sheer hard work. He may not have been blessed with the natural talent of playing contemporaries like Rodney Marsh, Stan Bowles or Tony Currie but he was a greater success than all of them.

From his first tentative steps as a professional at Scunthorpe United it was obvious that Keegan was different. At 15 he would run up and down the terraces with weights on his shoulders emulating the hardest, toughest player at the club.
"If he still did it to stay at the top, I knew I had to do it to get there," he later said.

His talent was spotted by the great Liverpool manager Bill Shankly who paid 35,000 pounds ($59,200) for his services in May 1971. He formed a marvellous attacking partnership with John Toshack which brought Liverpool glory and Keegan an England place. With Shankly as his mentor Keegan progressed to the heights. He said recently that no-one had an effect on him like Shankly, who died in 1981.
"I still think about him and his principles every single day of my life," he said.

And it was "pure Shankly" that Keegan displayed when he stood on the steps outside Newcastle's entrance and debated his decision to sell the club's leading scorer to their chief rivals with an angry mob of 300 fans. That's what Keegan did after letting Andy Cole leave for Manchester United for 7.0 million pounds two years ago this week.
As a player he exemplified an age when a youngster could become a mega-earning star through dedication and application on the pitch and astute business acumen off it.

His single-minded determination surfaced at Wembley in 1974 when Keegan refused to be subdued by Leeds firebrand Billy Bremner in the FA Charity Shield match. An inevitable clash led to both players being sent off, ripping off their shirts and throwing them to the pitch in protest as they departed.
The Football Association reacted with fury, fining the players 500 pounds each and banning them for a month.

Two months earlier Keegan had been involved in another headline-capturing incident. He was beaten up by airport officials and police as England arrived at Belgrade airport a few days before facing Yugoslavia.

Keegan took another beating in April 1991. After dropping out of sight to a Spanish retirement home for several years he was back on the front pages, victim of a mugging as he rested in his car at a Surrey car park.
Three thugs set about him with baseball bats, robbed him of 600 pounds and a credit card and left him dazed and bleeding. They were subsequently jailed for three years.

Keegan ended his playing career back in the north of England at Newcastle, who he helped gain promotion to the top division in 1984 which is why he was greeted as a Messiah when he returned as manager nearly five years ago.

Keegan set himself a number of personal goals and achieved almost all of them. But the "big one" got away. His critics would say his inability to win a single top-flight trophy in his five years as Newcastle manager will mark him down as a failure.
Keegan would say he entertained and thrilled a million Geordies with a team which knew only one way -- going forward.
But he spent nearly 60 million pounds and the Newcastle cupboard is still bare. Whatever Keegan says, that's why he has paid the ultimate price. ($ = 0.592 British Pounds)
